Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, either alone or in combination with emtricitabine, is recommended for use as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV transmission across diverse settings and populations. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) endorses the dapivirine vaginal ring as a novel option for HIV prevention in women at substantial risk of HIV infection. 3. For post-exposure prophylaxis, a two-drug regimen is effective; however, a three-drug regimen consisting of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, lamivudine (or emtricitabine), and dolutegravir is preferred. 4. As countries expand antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage, ART initiation should adhere to the principle of providing people-centered care. 5. Rapid ART initiation should be offered to individuals living with HIV immediately after a confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment. ART should be initiated on the same day for those ready to start treatment. 6. Implementing the recommendations in these guidelines will significantly impact program priorities, funding, and service delivery. 7. Service delivery guidance, as included in the 2016 guidelines, continues to assist countries in adopting new approaches and strengthening the treatment cascade. 8. The guidelines emphasize differentiated care for individuals established on ART, such as reducing clinic visit frequency and implementing community-based ART distribution. 9. These efficiencies aim to reduce the burden on both patients receiving treatment and healthcare facilities. 10. The guidelines also provide recommendations for initiating ART outside healthcare facilities and strategies for tracing and re-engaging individuals in care. 11. The consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery, and monitoring were revised following WHO Guideline Review Committee procedures. 12. New clinical and operational recommendations are based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, expert consultations, and country case studies. 13. The guideline development process has identified critical knowledge gaps to guide future HIV research. 14. The primary audience for these guidelines includes national HIV program managers in lowand middle-income countries, as well as clinicians and healthcare providers, particularly those in primary care settings. 15. The guidelines are also relevant to national HIV treatment advisory boards, HIV and TB program managers, communityand faith-based organizations, and international agencies providing technical and financial support to HIV programs in resource-limited settings. 16. People living with HIV, communities, and civil society organizations should be meaningfully engaged to support the successful implementation of these guidelines. 17. The COVID-19 pandemic has further delayed global efforts to end the HIV epidemic as a public health threat by 2030. 18. COVID-19 has disrupted services for HIV, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections, and harm reduction, with many countries reporting interruptions in HIV services during the pandemic's peak. 19. The full impact of COVID-19 will become clearer as additional clinical, epidemiological, and psychosocial data emerge. 20. The 2021 consolidated HIV guidelines represent a significant step toward achieving universal access to antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV, with the ultimate goal of ending the HIV epidemic as a major public health threat by 2030. 21. In high HIV-burden settings, HIV testing should be offered to all populations and integrated into various services, such as those for sexually transmitted infections, hepatitis, tuberculosis, malnutrition, antenatal care, and key populations. 22. Infants and children with unknown HIV status admitted for inpatient care or attending malnutrition clinics in high HIV-burden settings should be routinely tested for HIV. 23. HIV testing should also be offered in outpatient or immunization clinics for infants and children with unknown HIV status in high HIV-burden settings. 24. Biological children of parents living with HIV (or who may have died from HIV) should be routinely offered HIV testing services. If found to be infected or at high risk of infection, they should be linked to treatment or prevention services and provided with a broader package of voluntary provider-assisted referral. 25. Community-based HIV testing services are recommended, with linkage to prevention, treatment, and care services, in addition to routine facility-based testing, particularly for key populations. 26. HIV self-testing should be offered as an approach to HIV testing, with individuals receiving further testing from trained personnel if a reactive result is obtained. 27. Provider-assisted referral should be offered to people with HIV as part of a comprehensive package of testing and care. 28. Social network-based approaches can be used as an HIV testing strategy for key populations as part of a comprehensive care and prevention package. 29. Pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once and as early as possible during pregnancy. 30. Dual HIV and syphilis rapid diagnostic tests can be used as the first test in HIV testing strategies and algorithms in antenatal care. 31. Couples and partners should be offered voluntary HIV testing services with support for mutual disclosure. 32. Women disclosing violence by an intimate partner or sexual assault should be offered immediate support, including first-line support from healthcare providers. 33. Healthcare providers should assess exposure to intimate partner violence when evaluating conditions potentially caused or complicated by such violence to improve diagnosis and care. 34. Mandatory or coercive HIV testing is never justified. Providers should assess the risk of harm in consultation with the client.
